title: How BIM Adoption Changes Hiring Structure in Companies?{{year}}
summary: Discover how BIM is changing hiring processes, and skills required across AEC firms. Identify key roles that will merge in the future of work.
body_markdown:
## **Why Does BIM Adoption Changes How AEC Firms Hire and Organise Teams?**


****


BIM has introduced a different way of working, where project teams need a broader combination of technical expertise, BIM coordination skills, and digital capabilities. Here’s why:


**Tech-Pro Roles:** BIM workflows have created new positions such as BIM Coordinators, BIM Managers,


[BIM Modellers](https://www.novatr.com/blog/how-to-become-a-bim-modeler) , and Information Managers. These professionals take ownership of tasks that were previously distributed across traditional architecture, engineering, and project management roles.


**Greater Subject Matter Expertise:** Working on BIM-led projects requires more than knowing a modelling software. Professionals must understand model development, documentation, clash detection, coordination, and data exchange across various project stages.


**Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration:** BIM connects architectural, structural, MEP, and other project disciplines within a shared digital environment. This demands professionals who can communicate across teams and resolve issues rather than working in silos.


**Project-Based Experience:** Firms value candidates who can demonstrate how they have applied BIM skills to real projects. Experience with BIM standards and ISO 19650 protocol, model coordination, documentation, and delivery workflows can indicate whether a candidate is ready to contribute from day one.


**Digital Project Delivery:** BIM has shifted design and build workflows from manual processes towards connected digital workflows. Therefore, firms need professionals who can work with tools such as Revit,


[Navisworks](https://www.novatr.com/blog/navisworks-type) , ArchiCAD, Autodesk Construction Cloud, and Common Data Environments (CDEs).


**New Team Structures:** Traditional AEC teams often followed a straightforward hierarchy based on disciplines and seniority. However, BIM introduces new functions that create interconnected teams where experts work closely across different stages of delivery.


## **How Does BIM Adoption Influence Hiring Priorities and Team Structures?**


The changing nature of digital construction is pushing AEC firms to look beyond traditional roles when hiring and organising their teams. Here’s how this impacts BIM hiring across the domain:


**Hiring for BIM-Specific Roles:** Firms that once hired primarily around traditional architecture, engineering, and drafting positions now recruit for dedicated BIM roles. This has created positions such as BIM Coordinators,


[BIM Managers](https://www.novatr.com/blog/guide-to-become-bim-manager) , and Information Managers within larger teams.


**Prioritising Digital Competencies:** In workforce planning, the criteria have expanded beyond conventional design and engineering knowledge. Employers now assess candidates for their ability to work with BIM platforms, coordinate models, manage information, and navigate digital project environments.


**Valuing Practical Project Experience:** BIM proficiency on paper does not always indicate workplace readiness. Firms increasingly look for candidates who have applied their knowledge to live or simulated projects, handled coordination issues, followed project standards, and delivered BIM outputs.


**Moving Towards Multidisciplinary Teams:** Traditional teams were typically organised around separate disciplines, with coordination happening between them. BIM brings these disciplines into more connected workflows, increasing the need for professionals who can collaborate across architectural, structural, MEP, and other teams.


**Creating BIM-Specific Functions:** Larger AEC firms may establish BIM or digital delivery roles instead of distributing every BIM responsibility among existing staff. These teams can support multiple projects through coordination, standards, modelling, and technical assistance.


**Adding Coordination Layers:** BIM can introduce coordination functions between discipline teams and project leadership. This helps firms onboard professionals responsible for managing model integration, resolving conflicts, and keeping information aligned across teams.


**Bringing BIM Into Leadership:** At the senior level, the scope for BIM recruitment can advance into strategy and decision-making. BIM leaders may also oversee standards,


[digital workflows](https://www.novatr.com/blog/top-revit-features-for-better-design-and-bim-workflows) ,


technology implementation, and the organisation-wide use of BIM.


**Formalising Information Management:** The need to control project information has also created clearer responsibilities around data, CDEs, information requirements, and ISO 19650 processes. This gives information management a more defined place within modern AEC team structures.

## **What Challenges Do AEC Firms Face When Scaling BIM Teams?**


****


A pressing need for BIM expertise also brings challenges for firms trying to build and manage larger, capable BIM teams. Let’s explore the key issues in BIM implementation:


**Talent Shortages:** The rising demand for


[BIM professionals](https://www.novatr.com/blog/complete-bim-guide-for-aec-professionals) can make it difficult for firms to find candidates with the right skill set. Hiring someone who comprehends a BIM tool is often easier than finding someone who understands how to apply it within real project workflows.


**Upgrading Existing Teams:** Incorporating BIM across a set workforce needs professionals to learn new tools, processes, and responsibilities. Firms must invest in continuous training while helping employees apply these skills to active projects without disrupting ongoing work.


**Change Management:** Moving from familiar 2D or fragmented workflows to a connected BIM environment can meet resistance from teams accustomed to existing processes. Successful implementation needs proactive communication, leadership support, and adequate time for employees to adapt.


**Process Standardisation:** Larger teams need uniform modelling standards, naming conventions, and documentation practices. Without clearly defined processes, different teams may develop their own methods, making information more difficult to manage.


**Cross-Functional Collaboration:** BIM brings architects, engineers, contractors, and other specialists into close-knit collaboration. While this can improve project delivery, it also requires teams to communicate effectively,


[resolve conflicts](https://www.novatr.com/blog/clash-detection-and-resolution-in-mep-projects) , and understand how their work affects other disciplines.
